content: I'm pretty new to lean, the docs on "Finite" say it should be preferred over Fintype unless necessary for some computations, but working on formalizing some results and concepts in graph theory and noticed that there are quite a few instances of theorems or definitions with SimpleGraph using Fintype rather than Finite, even when there don't appear to be any uses of the computability aspect of a Fintype. I'm wondering if this is a case of an older style, but Finite should be preferred now when possible, or if Fintype is really to be preferred here (to avoid needing adding Fintype.ofFinite before reasoning about cardinalities or similar). Or is it something else entirely?

Hello :wave:
When possible, prefer Finite over Fintype. Mathlib also has a linter for this :)
Do you have an example of theorems where it seems that the Fintype is unused? It's usually used for Fintype.card or Set.toFinset (which includes using stuff like SimpleGraph.neighborFinset or SimpleGraph.degree).
See also #mathlib4 > Order and size of a graph @ 💬 about Fintype.card.

Christopher Aagaard said:

I'm wondering if this is a case of an older style

I think Fintype.card was a thing before Nat.card/ENat.card/Cardinal.mk/Set.ncard/Set.encard so it is an older style, although computability of graph stuff can be useful: SimpleGraph/Finite.lean contains a bunch of stuff for computability so intentionally uses Fintype.

Hi!
The linter telling me not to use a Fintype was what had lead me to the Finite docs and then to wonder about choosing for defs since the linter doesn't care about them :)

I don't think this was one of the examples I noticed the yesterday, but in the SimpleGraph.DegreeSum I think dart_fst_fiber only uses Fintype to get a Finset, and now I'm thinking this may be the real style question I'm trying to understand: Since the computability isn't being used here, if this theorem hadn't already been in Mathlib and I was going to write it, would the best practice be to only require Finite and use Fintype.ofFinite or to just require a Fintype as it currently is?

Specifically to sum over a set we usually use docs#Finset.sum, so without a Fintype we can't really sum over all the vertices in the graph (even if degree didn't require Fintype).
We could state it with Finite if we use docs#finsum, which could be nice.
Though I think that the degree-sum formula is essentially about an equivalence between darts and all the neighbor sets, which I (trivially) formalized but apparently forgot to PR:

/-- There is a bijection between the darts of a graph and the disjoint union of all neighbor sets -/
@[simps]
def dartEquivSigmaNeighborSet : G.Dart ≃ Σ v, G.neighborSet v where
  toFun d := ⟨d.fst, d.snd, d.adj⟩
  invFun v := ⟨(v.fst, v.snd), v.snd.property⟩
  left_inv d := by simp
  right_inv v := by simp

Then you could get statements about cardinalities from it without assuming Fintype

btw you might like:

  • #36406 shows Cardinal.mk G.Dart = 2 * Cardinal.mk G.edgeSet in matchings (no Fintype)
  • #33501 adds SimpleGraph.edegree which doesn't require Fintype
  • docs#SimpleGraph.isTree_iff_connected_and_card is a nice statement which uses Nat.card so it can require Finite instead of Fintype (and the matching #34910)

For the last one I think the correct generality is an equivalence V ≃ G.edgeSet ⊕ G.ConnectedComponent without any cardinalities. (I have some progress locally but it's not trivial.)
Ah, thank you! That makes sense to me. Those links even answer some of the questions I hadn't gotten to asking yet (like how to use Finiteness effectively without adding a Fintype.ofFinite) :)
